title: Extreme Heat Is Already Dangerous to Americans. The Super El Niño Could Make Next Year Worse.
text:
Extreme Heat Is Already Dangerous to Americans. The Super El Niño Could Make Next Year Worse.

Photo: Frederic J. BROWN / AFP via Getty Images

Critical Questions
by

Caitlin Noe
and
Sophia Hirshfield

Published November 20, 2026

This year’s global climate summit, COP31, took place in Turkey against the backdrop of a Super El Niño, a particularly strong climate phenomenon that can drastically change global weather patterns. Despite this looming threat—which early analysis suggests will drive nearly half a million global deaths from extreme heat alone—the United States declined to send an official delegation to the event for the second year in a row, reflecting its wholesale deprioritization of climate issues in recent years. In the United States, extreme heat events are becoming more frequent, more intense, and longer lasting. Extreme heat is already the deadliest weather-related hazard in the United States and kills more people than floods, tornadoes, and hurricanes combined. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that extreme heat claims around 1,700 lives annually in the United States, though this is likely a severe undercount, and the toll could be as high as 10,000 annually. Vulnerable populations such as the elderly, young children, and the chronically ill suffer disproportionately, but the shared experience of extreme heat cuts across political identity, economic status, and geography.Heat from the Super El Niño phenomenon, when combined with the impacts of climate change, raises the possibility that summer 2027 could set a new heat record. The arrival of new congressional members in January may provide an opportunity for Congress to push forward more bipartisan action on measures that better protect Americans. The incoming Congress should take three steps to combat the health consequences of extreme heat: (1) press for the formulation of a national heat response plan; (2) strengthen and sustain key data resources at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to inform national planning; and (3) expand critical Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) response resources to better reinforce the patchwork of state and local efforts and ensure that all Americans are adequately protected.Q1: What are the consequences of extreme heat for Americans?A1: Widespread public worry about extreme heat is rooted in people’s lived experience. The June 2025 heat dome exposed more than 255 million Americans to extreme heat conditions. A 2026 survey found that U.S. adults are more likely to say extreme heat has impacted their travel or vacation plans, electricity bills, sleep, outdoor activities, or other parts of their day-to-day lives than in July 2024.Exposure to extreme heat has a growing and underestimated effect on Americans’ health. Some individuals experience mild reactions such as heat rash and muscle cramps, or moderate impacts including exhaustion, lack of energy, headache, and dizziness. In severe cases, extreme heat can lead to heatstroke, which, when left untreated, can cause organ damage and death. Between 1999 and 2023, 21,518 deaths in the United States were reported with heat as an underlying or contributing cause of death. The annual extreme heat death toll increased by 117 percent in 2023 compared with 1999. Some experts indicate that the death toll is severely undercounted and that extreme heat kills five times more people than official statistics illustrate.Extreme heat can also exacerbate the consequences of chronic health conditions such as cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, diabetes, and asthma; contribute to adverse birth outcomes and respiratory infections; increase the incidence of certain infectious diseases; and aggravate mental health disorders. The health impacts of extreme heat are particularly acute for certain vulnerable populations, including outdoor workers, people experiencing homelessness, pregnant individuals, and people with preexisting conditions. The elderly, young children, and those with chronic medical conditions are at especially high risk for heat-related illness and death. There is a continued need for greater investment in biomedical research on the health impacts of extreme heat and options for mitigation, especially for vulnerable individuals.Q2: What is a Super El Niño, and how might it contribute to extreme heat across the United States?A2: El Niño refers to a natural phenomenon that occurs when higher-than-average water temperatures in the Pacific Ocean shift wind patterns and ultimately change global weather patterns. The weather pattern occurs every two to seven years and lasts nine to twelve months. A Super El Niño refers to an especially strong El Niño cycle, often used to describe events where the average sea temperature is at least 3 degrees Celsius higher than average. On June 11, NOAA forecasted this season’s El Niño to intensify in the Northern Hemisphere in the winter of 2026–27, and in September the Super El Niño officially became the strongest ever recorded. Forecasts from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) indicate an “exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100%” that El Niño will persist through February 2027.  While the Super El Niño is expected to complete its cycle in the winter months, the changes in the jet stream from El Niño can temporarily boost overall global temperatures during the spring and summer months. The phenomenon will almost certainly make 2027 the hottest year on record in the United States when compounded by human-caused climate change, the primary driver behind record-breaking global temperatures. Though impacts will vary by country and region, the WMO advises countries and communities to prepare for increased health risks due to the potential of El Niño to contribute to extreme heat.Q3: What is the United States already doing to prepare, and where are the gaps in preparedness?A3: In summer 2025, the National Weather Service issued heat advisories for every region of the continental United States and Alaska for the first time. However, the United States has no active national extreme heat plan, relying instead on a patchwork of actions from federal agencies and state and local governments. Meaningful progress in addressing extreme heat has been made by individual agencies and at the state and local levels, but efforts are uneven, fragmented, and often unsustainable due to limited state and federal support.Although FEMA’s core mission is to coordinate federal disaster response and recovery efforts, extreme heat is not explicitly cited within its mandate. The National Integrated Heat Health Information System (NIHHIS) was established as part of NOAA to provide risk forecasting on extreme heat. Although the NIHHIS’s interagency working group developed a National Heat Strategy for 2024–2030, that plan was taken offline in 2025 by the Trump administration, and the co-chairs of the working group have since left government and have not been replaced. Since 2025, federal funding for domestic climate agencies and programs has been slashed, and the Trump administration’s 2027 budget proposal includes even deeper proposed cuts—including for NOAA and FEMA.State policymakers increasingly recognize the health threats posed by extreme heat, but public health interventions vary widely, including in the division of resources between preparedness and response capabilities. Some states provide emergency response services or medical assistance for the uninsured or underinsured. Other states have implemented prevention measures, including heat awareness campaigns and cooling centers, as well as climate data and mapping tools to identify high-risk populations. Others are beginning to develop and implement heat action plans, and a few have appointed heat officers statewide.At the local level, Miami-Dade County, Los Angeles, and Phoenix have established heat response officers or offices, and 11 U.S. cities have taken steps to address extreme heat. Local and state governments often remain constrained in their efforts by uncertain state and federal support. In a 2025 survey, more than half of local public health associations said that barriers to addressing heat included competing priorities and a lack of funding for and understanding of heat-related solutions.Q4: What more can Congress do to prepare for the health impacts of extreme heat?A4: The incoming Congress should take three key actions on a bipartisan basis to further strengthen federal functions that cannot be fulfilled by other levels of government, and that are needed to mitigate the potential health impacts of extreme heat on Americans.First, Congress should establish a commission to develop an updated national heat response plan to provide clarity around local, state, and federal functions; define what actions would best strengthen extreme heat preparedness and response; and set priorities for future extreme heat funding. Legislation has already been introduced in both the House and Senate to establish an interagency committee to coordinate federal heat response efforts, but neither bill has passed. The Congressional Extreme Heat Caucus co-chairs recently introduced the Extreme Heat Congressional Advisory Commission Act, which could offer an opportunity to strengthen national policy over time.Second, Congress should sustain and staff NOAA’s NIHHIS to ensure that federal, state, and local actors; civil society organizations; the private sector; and academia all have easy and timely access to the data they need to make evidence-based decisions that protect their constituents from extreme heat. The NIHHIS and its interagency working group play a pivotal role in supplying heat-related data to state, local, and international partners—a centralized responsibility that cannot be replaced in full by a patchwork of local actors.Third, Congress should strengthen FEMA capabilities and authorities to explicitly account for extreme heat risks and better support states and localities in assessing, planning for, and responding to extreme heat events. FEMA can work with NOAA to assess vulnerabilities and determine where to target resources to build preparedness at the state and local levels; provide rapid-response support in extreme heat emergencies; and provide grants to fund operational costs of local resilience hubs, cooling centers, and hospital surge capacity.As the 120th Congress begins in 2027, there is a window of opportunity to forge a bipartisan consensus around actionable steps to combat the rising health threats of extreme heat. Congressional momentum and action will in turn support state and local leaders across the country who have already begun to address the threat extreme heat poses to Americans’ health. Coordinated efforts at the national, state, and local levels will give Americans a better defense against the extreme heat coming next year.Caitlin Noe is a program coordinator with the Global Health Policy Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington, D.C. Sophia Hirshfield is an associate fellow with the CSIS Global Health Policy Center.The authors would like to thank J. Stephen Morrison, Katherine E.
